newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-AKINWANDE AND ZOLKIN FINALLY GET WORLDWIDE EXPOSURE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-AKINWANDE AND ZOLKIN FINALLY GET WORLDWIDE EXPOSURE.

text.p: Britain's Henry Akinwande and Russian Alexander Zolkin will get the worldwide exposure they have been fighting for when they meet for the little-known World Boxing Organisation (WBO) heavyweight title Saturday as part of the Mike Tyson-Evander Holyfield card.

"People just don't know about Henry, but the kid can fight, he has speed, power, he has the whole package," Akinwande's manager George Kanter said of the undefeated Briton, who is making his first title defence.

A sellout crowd of 16,000 at the MGM Grand and a global television audience of millions are expected to watch Tyson defend his World Boxing Association (WBA) crown against Holyfield, a former two-time champion.
Zolkin will make people take notice of his toughness, said John Johnson, manager of the Russian-born challenger, who moved to the United States five years ago.
"I would put him up against anybody in the street or in the ring and he would show up first," Johnson said of Zolkin. "He is going to make history by becoming the first Russian heavyweight champion."
Akinwande, 30-0-1, who won the vacant title by stopping Jeremy Williams in the third round four months ago, is listed a slight 5-2 betting favourite.

"He hasn't had to face a fighter who has my speed," said the 6-foot-7 (2.01 metres) Akinwande, whose 85-inch (2.16 metres) reach could help him keep Zolkin away with his jab. "I don't want to let him set the pace, so I'll jab him and use my boxing ability and I think that will put the fight my way."
Johnson sees it differently, of course.
"We are totally confident," said Johnson, who managed James "Buster" Douglas when he shook the world by knocking out Tyson in 1990. "Akinwande is a really good fighter, but great beats really good."
Said Zolkin: "I don't fear anybody, I'm not scared of anybody, I just come to fight."
Both fighters have come a long way to get their biggest paydays of their careers, $250,000 for Akinwande and $200,000 for Zolkin.
Zolkin, 32, grew up on the mean streets of Moscow before leaving six years ago to begin his pro career.
"This is what I have dreamed of, that some day, some day I'm going to be there," Zolkin said of getting his first title shot.
"The kid came up really tough, he had it tougher than most any American ever," Johnson said.
"He didn't have enough food to eat, he could have gone to a mental institution for talking about religion, he could have gone to jail for spitting on the street," Johnson said.

Akinwande, 31, was born in Britain but his parents took him back to their native Nigeria when he was a child. He returned to England against his father's wishes in 1989 to start his fighting career, and struggled to make ends meet as a London street cleaner.
"He is in place to fight the best now, the only thing that can stop it is if he loses," said Kanter.
